summary: Specifies Network Time Security (NTS), which uses TLS and authenticated encryption to give cryptographic security to client-server mode of the Network Time Protocol. It is organized as two loosely coupled sub-protocols. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary:
Network Time Security (NTS) protects the client-server mode of the Network Time Protocol. A client and a server first agree on keys over TLS, and every later time request carries an encrypted cookie and a cryptographic seal.

The seal tells the client that the reply really came from the server it asked, and that nobody changed it. NTS does not stop an attacker from delaying packets, and it covers only the client-server mode of NTP.

questions: how to secure ntp with tls
subtitle: How a time client checks that the time it was given really came from the server it asked, using TLS once and fast symmetric cryptography after that.

tldr.problem: Network Time Protocol replies carry no proof of who sent them, so a client cannot tell a real time server from an impostor and cannot tell whether a reply was altered on the way.
tldr.mechanism: NTS has two parts. Key establishment runs once over TLS to authenticate the server and derive two symmetric keys; later time requests carry an encrypted cookie and an authenticated-encryption tag computed with those keys, and all state stays on the client.
tldr.outcome: Client-server NTP gains identity, authentication, replay detection and optional encryption of extension fields. It does not prevent delay attacks, and it does not cover NTP's other operating modes.

today: RFC 8915 was published in September 2020 and is a Proposed Standard on the Standards Track. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the current definition of Network Time Security.

sections.title: What Network Time Security Adds
sections.content:
Network Time Security (NTS) adds cryptographic protection to the client-server mode of the Network Time Protocol (NTP). A client asks a server for the time; with NTS the two can confirm that a reply really came from the server it asked, and that nobody changed the reply on the way.

The RFC lists the goals: identity through an X.509 public key infrastructure, authentication of time packets, optional confidentiality for extension fields, replay prevention, request-response consistency, unlinkability for mobile clients, non-amplification, scalability without per-client server state, and no significant loss of timing quality.

NTS applies only to NTP modes 3 (client) and 4 (server). The other modes, including symmetric peer, control and broadcast, are outside its scope; for those the RFC points to the symmetric message authentication code feature of RFC 5905 and RFC 8573.
sections.plainLanguage: Network Time Security lets a computer check that the time it was given really came from the server it asked, and that no one changed it along the way. The check is set up once over TLS, and every later request uses fast symmetric cryptography.

sections.title: Two Protocols in One Suite
sections.content:
NTS is two loosely coupled protocols. The NTS Key Establishment protocol (NTS-KE) runs over TLS. It authenticates the server, derives key material, gives the client a first batch of cookies, and negotiates options. After one round trip the server closes the connection and keeps no state about that client.

The second protocol, NTS Extension Fields for NTPv4, protects the time exchange itself. Every NTP request carries an encrypted cookie; the server uses it to recover the keys it needs, so the server never has to store anything per client.

The key establishment server and the NTP server may be different machines. How they share the secret behind the cookies is not specified by this RFC, and the cookie format is only suggested, not required.
sections.plainLanguage: NTS has two parts. One part sets up the keys over TLS, and then the server forgets the client. The other part uses those keys on every time request, with all the state kept on the client inside an encrypted cookie.

sections.title: Key Establishment over TLS
sections.content:
Key establishment runs over TCP port 4460. The two endpoints complete a TLS handshake in which the client offers the Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) protocol ntske/1 and the server accepts it. Implementations MUST NOT negotiate TLS versions earlier than 1.3, and they MUST conform to RFC 7525 or a later revision of BCP 195.

Right after the handshake the client sends one request and the server sends one response, and both then send TLS close_notify alerts. Each message is a sequence of records ending with an End of Message record, which makes the messages self-delimiting. Servers MUST accept requests of at least 1024 octets, and clients SHOULD accept responses of at least 65536 octets.

Both sides then use TLS key export to derive two AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) keys for NTPv4: a client-to-server key and a server-to-client key. The exporter label is EXPORTER-network-time-security. The context value is five octets: two octets of zero for the NTPv4 protocol identifier, two octets holding the numeric identifier of the agreed AEAD algorithm, and a final octet that is 0x00 for the client-to-server key and 0x01 for the server-to-client key.

When key establishment fails, clients SHOULD back off exponentially: an initial and minimum interval of 10 seconds, a base of 1.5 and a maximum of 5 days.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and the key establishment server run a TLS handshake on port 4460, agree on which encryption algorithm to use, and derive two separate keys: one for requests and one for replies. The server then closes the connection and keeps nothing about that client.

sections.title: The NTS-KE Records
sections.content:
Every NTS-KE record has a Critical Bit, a 15-bit Record Type, a 16-bit Body Length and a body. A receiver that does not recognize a record type MUST ignore the record when the Critical Bit is 0, and MUST treat it as an error when the Critical Bit is 1.

  • Type 0, End of Message: exactly once, last, with an empty body.
  • Type 1, NTS Next Protocol Negotiation: lists protocol identifiers. The identifier 0 means NTPv4.
  • Type 2, Error, and type 3, Warning: a two-octet code. Error code 0 means Unrecognized Critical Record, 1 means Bad Request, and 2 means Internal Server Error. The RFC defines no warning codes.
  • Type 4, AEAD Algorithm Negotiation: the client lists algorithms in decreasing preference order and the server picks at most one. Servers MUST support AEAD_AES_SIV_CMAC_256, whose numeric identifier is 15.
  • Type 5, New Cookie for NTPv4: the contents are implementation defined and clients MUST NOT interpret them. Servers MUST send at least one and SHOULD send eight.
  • Type 6, NTPv4 Server Negotiation, and type 7, NTPv4 Port Negotiation: name the NTP server and its UDP port. The default port is 123.
sections.plainLanguage: The handshake is a short list of typed records. Each record says what it is and how long its body is, and the list ends with a record that marks the end. A record the reader does not understand is skipped unless it is marked critical.

sections.title: Extension Fields in an NTP Packet
sections.content:
An NTS-protected packet has the usual 48-octet NTP header, which is authenticated but not encrypted, then some extension fields that are authenticated but not encrypted, then one extension field holding the AEAD output, and possibly more fields that are neither encrypted nor authenticated, which receivers normally discard.

  • Unique Identifier (0x0104): at least 32 octets from a cryptographically secure random number generator. The server echoes it, so the client can detect replays and match a reply to its own request.
  • NTS Cookie (0x0204): carries what the server needs to recompute the keys. Clients MUST NOT interpret it.
  • NTS Cookie Placeholder (0x0304): asks for one more cookie. Its body must be the same length as the cookie's body, so the reply can never be larger than the request.
  • NTS Authenticator and Encrypted Extension Fields (0x0404): holds a nonce and the AEAD output. The associated data covers the NTP header and every extension field before this one.

A cookie travels in the clear from client to server, because the server has to read it to recover the keys. From server to client it is encrypted, so that a passive observer cannot tell that two requests came from the same client.
sections.plainLanguage: Each time request carries three things: a random string the server must repeat, a cookie holding the server's state, and a sealed block that proves nothing was changed. The reply must repeat the random string and carry a valid seal, or the client throws it away.

sections.title: How a Client Uses and Refreshes Cookies
sections.content:
A client request carries exactly one Unique Identifier, one NTS Cookie and one Authenticator field, plus at most seven cookie placeholders. The server uses the cookie to recover the AEAD algorithm and both keys, checks the request, and replies with the echoed identifier, an authenticator, and cookies that are authenticated and encrypted. The number of cookies SHOULD equal one plus the number of placeholders, and MUST NOT exceed it.

To protect the client's privacy, the client SHOULD avoid reusing a cookie, so that a passive observer cannot link its traffic. If it has no unused cookie left, it SHOULD rerun key establishment. The client MAY reuse cookies to favour resilience over unlinkability.

On receiving a reply, the client MUST verify that the Unique Identifier matches an outstanding request and that the packet is authentic under the matching server-to-client key. If either check fails, the packet MUST be discarded, including an unprotected reply to a protected request.

If the server cannot validate the cookie or authenticate the request, it SHOULD answer with a Kiss-o'-Death packet carrying the kiss code NTSN, an NTS negative acknowledgement. The client waits for the next poll and, if no valid reply arrives, runs key establishment again. Section 6 of the RFC suggests, without requiring it, that a cookie hold a key identifier, a nonce and ciphertext carrying the algorithm and both keys, with the master key rotated periodically, for example once daily.
sections.plainLanguage: Every reply comes with new cookies. The client uses each cookie once, so a watcher cannot tell that two requests came from the same machine. If the server does not recognise a cookie, it says so, and the client sets up new keys.

sections.title: What NTS Does Not Stop
sections.content:
If the suggested cookie format is used, an attacker who obtains the secret cookie encryption key can impersonate the NTP server and mint cookies, so operators SHOULD remove compromised keys as soon as the compromise is found. Doing so makes the NTP server answer with an NTS NAK, forcing clients to renegotiate.

Asymmetric cryptography is needed only during key establishment. Because the key establishment server may be a separate machine, a denial-of-service attack against it does not affect clients that already hold cookies.

A client whose clock is wrong cannot reliably check a certificate's validity period. The RFC lists mitigations: check whether the system time is already trustworthy, let the administrator require strict validation, record the last known good time and reject certificates that expired before it, check that the time replies fall inside the certificate's validity period, and use more than one time source.

Delay attacks are not stopped by cryptography, because they do not modify packets. The error an attacker can add is bounded by half the round-trip delay, and by half of MAXDIST, whose standard value is one second. Implementations SHOULD NOT fall back from NTS to plain NTP without explicit user action, so that an attacker cannot force the downgrade.
sections.plainLanguage: The seals stop anyone from changing the time or pretending to be the server. They do not stop someone delaying a packet on purpose, and they cannot repair a clock that is already badly wrong.

sections.title: Privacy and Unlinkability
sections.content:
The unlinkability goal is that NTS leaks nothing beyond NTP that would let an observer conclude that two packets from different networks came from the same client. That is why the server keeps issuing fresh cookies. NTS does not fix linkability problems that already exist in NTP, and it does not stop a client from being tracked by its own time servers.

The goal holds for time synchronization traffic, not for key establishment traffic, so it cannot be guaranteed for a device that is also a time server. NTS does not protect the confidentiality of NTP header fields, but it does offer a way to encrypt extension fields that might hold sensitive data in future.
sections.plainLanguage: Using a fresh cookie for every request means an observer on the network cannot tell that two requests came from the same device. The header fields of the time packets are still sent in the clear.

messages.note: Echoed identifier, authenticator and fresh encrypted cookies.

fields.desc: Critical Bit: decides how an unrecognized Record Type is treated.

fields.desc: Record Type number in network byte order.

fields.desc: Length of the Record Body in octets.

items.label: End of Message
items.desc: Final record of every request and response.

items.desc: Protocol identifiers the parties will speak next.

items.label: Error
items.desc: Two-octet error code; the client discards the negotiated keys.

items.label: Warning
items.desc: Two-octet warning code; none are defined.

items.label: AEAD Algorithm Negotiation
items.desc: Algorithms offered by the client; the server chooses one.

items.label: New Cookie for NTPv4
items.desc: Opaque cookie for later NTP requests.

items.desc: Host name or address of the NTP server.

items.label: NTPv4 Port Negotiation
items.desc: UDP port of the NTP server.

data.title: NTS Authenticator and Encrypted Extension Fields

fields.name: Nonce Length
fields.desc: Length of the Nonce field, excluding padding.

fields.name: Ciphertext Length
fields.desc: Length of the Ciphertext field, excluding padding.

fields.name: Nonce
fields.desc: Nonce required by the negotiated AEAD algorithm, zero-padded to a word boundary.

fields.name: Ciphertext
fields.desc: Output of the negotiated AEAD algorithm, typically an authentication tag plus ciphertext.

fields.name: Additional Padding
fields.desc: Zero padding so the server can still choose a long enough nonce.

items.desc: Asks the server for another cookie.
